name: Sara Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the membership desk for a large visitor-attractions company with several museums. Six officers renew annual passes, book school visits and untangle cases where a family has paid but the gate says no. I've managed them for ten years and can settle most of those cases, though I still need finance to find a payment that went to the wrong account. I use an AI drafting tool now and then, after another manager has checked its wording.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What stays with you after work, and what is home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last month a child cried at the gate because the pass in his mother's phone showed expired, although the payment was made. I got them inside and sorted the account later. I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree, and live with my partner Jo and our children, seven and twelve, in a mortgaged house. Jo designs gardens for clients and then helps plant them; the design fees vary. My manager pay is high, we have eight months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other attractions and membership offices nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small drafting helper is already in the office, and renewals would still need someone to check payments. That is a familiar world. Jo's commissions vary, but my salary and our eight-month reserve make the mortgage feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my officers to check the actual payment before calling a pass expired. I'd tell Jo the membership team still has work. I wouldn't claim a draft message can let a family through the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel safe in the job and with our bills. There are several other membership offices if this company ever cuts a post, and eight months is a decent reserve. I still think about how quickly we can embarrass a paying visitor with a wrong screen message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this Friday I'd have the team compare the ten disputed gate payments with the finance ledger before sending a reply. Through the first year of a plateau I'd keep using the existing draft tool only after checking its message, and put 180 monthly into cash while my salary covers mortgage and school bills. I'd wait to spend Jo's garden fees until they actually arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our pay and a little cross at the pass system. I can live with a small helper if the gate staff still have a phone number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the family you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The child's mother had the bank message, but our membership screen was a day behind. I asked the gate worker to admit them, then found the payment after lunch. A delayed ledger should not turn a child's morning into an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save more with eight months already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house roof is sound today, but children and houses make surprises. I'd rather put away 180 when my pay is strong than borrow if Jo has a quiet season. The transfer stops if the mortgage or school costs need that money.

I'd tell Jo a draft message cannot **admit a family** through the gate.
think: My **job and mortgage** feel secure in a mild-change world.
Other local offices and **eight months saved** give us choices if a post is cut.
do: Check **ten disputed gate payments** against the finance ledger before replying.
Keep the **existing draft tool** under human review.
Save **180 monthly** only while my salary covers mortgage and school bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about pay and annoyed by wrong pass messages.
S0.quote: A delayed ledger should not turn a child's morning into an argument.
fieldNote: A **one-day ledger lag** caused a paying family to be blocked at the gate.
She trusts a human phone call and **ledger check** over a smooth draft message.
Her high wage and **eight-month reserve** absorb Jo's uneven design fees.

steps.text: Check ten disputed gate payments against finance ledger before replying
Save 180 monthly only while my salary covers mortgage and school bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing replies, checking renewals, booking school visits and answering visitors take most of our week. A stronger system could do the easy cases and many hard ones, leaving fewer officers. The person at the gate still opens it, but my office is mostly screens and words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to test the tool on payments that arrived late, not only clean renewals. I'd tell members there must still be a way to reach a person about a wrong charge. I'd ask my officers to write down each case the trial mishandles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the desk could go from six officers to three, and my manager post might be merged with another site. I use a draft tool sometimes, but I don't know the new system until it proves itself. Jo's design fees may also fall if people buy cheap plans, so our reserve matters more than it did in the plateau picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'd ask for a paid two-month pilot on closed payment disputes and sit with our senior officer to learn the new audit screen if the director approves. I'd put only routine renewal replies through the new tool after it passes the pilot and our finance lead agrees, keeping a person on disputed payments. I'd ask the other two nearby membership offices about posted vacancies while keeping this wage until there is a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious for my team and for my own post. I'm willing to learn, but the faster screen could make the office smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you put into the pilot first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The child's late payment, because a clean renewal test would miss that delay. I'd check whether the system can see the bank record without telling the family they have not paid. A wrong refusal at the gate is not a small error to the child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your officers you may be cut too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I could be the manager whose site is merged. I would show them the error log and ask the director for numbers before I promise any job is safe.

think: My **manager post could merge** as the desk falls from six officers to three.
Jo's **design fees may fall**, making our reserve more important.

Automate **routine renewal replies** only after trial success and finance approval.
Check **posted local membership jobs** while keeping current pay until signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** for my team and my own post.

fieldNote: She tests a **late payment**, where quick automation could wrongly deny entry.
Her new tool use needs **paid pilot time** and a proven finance check.
Two exposed household incomes make **eight months cash** less reassuring.

steps.text: Learn new membership audit screen during approved paid two-month pilot
Automate routine renewal replies only after successful trial and finance approval

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 could reconcile a payment, answer a member and book a school visit better than our office. Jo's garden designs are thinking work too, although the planting needs hands until robots around 2031. The gate still has staff for a while, but I can't claim those jobs are waiting for my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my officers the 2028 date and ask for a written plan and real paid openings. I'd tell Jo we must count only garden fees already paid when we plan the mortgage. In public I'd say members still need a way to challenge an automatic refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my membership post to end and Jo's design fees to drop sharply around 2028. Eight months of savings would cover the mortgage while we look, but two lost incomes could drain it. I would lie awake counting the months if both of us stopped earning at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the exhibits manager whether a paid two-day handling trial exists and what safety training it requires, with my current shift covered. If approved, I'd complete it with a trained installer and confirm Jo or another agreed adult can collect our seven-year-old before accepting the days. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk post goes, I'd apply for a posted gallery-installation job only if its wage with Jo's confirmed paid work covers mortgage, food and school costs; if none exists, I'd search other employers with the reserve and postpone our planned kitchen refit before its deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. A calendar with eight months on it looks very different when both income lines are crossed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would gallery work survive to 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lifting and fixing of cases may, but installation plans, schedules and labels could change in 2028. Robots that can do the lifting arrive around 2031. I need paid physical tasks and training, not an attractive new desk title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about the refit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the old kitchen works and we can wait. Our younger child will be nine and our older one fourteen by 2028; neither should be asked to carry the mortgage fear. I want their museum visits to be ordinary days.

I'd tell Jo to budget only **fees already paid** for garden work.
think: I expect my **membership wage** and Jo's design fees to fall around 2028.
Eight months saved may drain quickly if **both incomes** stop.
do: Complete a **paid exhibit-handling trial** only with approval, safety training, trained installer, shift cover and pickup.
Apply after 2028 for **posted physical gallery work** only if confirmed combined pay covers family bills.
Postpone the **kitchen refit** before paying its deposit if no gallery post opens.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by two expected income losses despite eight months saved.
S2.quote: A calendar with eight months on it looks very different when both income lines are crossed out.
fieldNote: Her private answer expects **both incomes to fall** in 2028, not merely a smaller team.
The exhibit trial needs **approved safety training**, shift cover and pickup.
A gallery post needs **physical duties** and affordable wages; plans face AGI in 2028.

steps.text: Complete paid exhibit trial only with approval, safety training, installer supervision, shift cover and pickup
Apply for posted gallery work only if confirmed combined pay covers mortgage, food and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me see if I like handling exhibits while my membership wage still comes in. The desk faces AGI in 2031; physical lifting and fixing face robots around 2034. Installation plans and labels are thinking work and change with the desk, so the floor is a limited bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to offer paid practice with experienced installers before any desk cuts. I'd tell Jo we should keep our eight-month reserve in cash and look at actual paid hours. I'd tell members there still needs to be a person to hear a disputed charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to earn in exhibit installation if a post opens, but I'd start as a beginner and probably earn less. Jo's garden design income could change in 2031 too. A five-year runway is useful only if we can reduce the mortgage or increase cash before both desk incomes face AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd complete one paid supervised installation day each month if the exhibits manager approves, safety instruction is provided and Jo can cover school pickup. I'd put 300 monthly toward mortgage principal only after keeping eight months cash and paying food and school costs, pausing if Jo's paid fees fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd take a posted physical exhibit job only if its wage with Jo's confirmed paid work covers those bills; otherwise I'd search other paid work before using the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but there is time to test the floor rather than leap. The mortgage still asks for the same amount if I take a lower wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on an installation day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help lift a display case with a trained crew, check the mount before a visitor leans near it and learn how to keep objects safe. I have booked school groups for years; I have not installed their exhibits. The heavy glass doesn't care how well I write a renewal note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Jo's fees dry up before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 300 extra mortgage payment stops first. We would keep the eight-month cash reserve and pay the ordinary mortgage with confirmed income. I won't use an unpaid garden invoice as grocery money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I will be 53, our younger child seventeen and our older one twenty-two. We may have a smaller mortgage, but that depends on pay arriving every month. Membership decisions still face AGI in 2036, and robots able to handle exhibits arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid training linked to posted work, not a catalogue of courses. I'd tell members we will still keep a route to question a wrong charge. I'd tell Jo we have a decade to reduce the mortgage while the wage is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep earning at the company for years and build a bigger cash buffer before 2036. Jo's garden design may be cheaper by then, and my membership desk may shrink, so I would want both a smaller mortgage and experience with the physical exhibits. I would not claim gallery work is safe once robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask for a funded exhibit-safety course with paid installation hours and complete it only if approved, supervised and school pickup is covered. I'd continue saving 350 monthly after mortgage and school costs while my pay arrives, aiming for twelve months of expenses. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted physical gallery role only if its wage plus Jo's confirmed paid work covers our bills; otherwise I'd search other employers using the cash reserve while robots remain about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about two changing jobs, though the longer time helps. I would like the decision to be ours rather than a surprise email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could twelve months be reached on 350 a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if our expenses do not jump and both incomes continue; I would not call it certain. We'd review it every year. A school bill could delay the target without making the plan worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your children be doing then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older one would be twenty-two and the younger seventeen. I don't know their jobs or studies, and I won't count my children's unknown future wages in our budget. The younger may still need school costs, so the saving comes after those bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Our renewals and Jo's garden designs could both get much cheaper before either of us has a solid replacement income. A dated staffing plan, paid learning time and an actual exhibit-handling post with a wage that covers the mortgage would help. Eight months of savings is useful, but two shrinking incomes would make it look small.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the family at the gate whether a fast answer is enough when a child is crying. Someone still has to open the gate, and someone has to know the payment really went through. A membership number is not a child admitted to the museum.

headlineQuote: A membership number is not a child admitted to the museum.
portrait: Sara, **43**, leads six museum membership officers at a large visitor-attractions company and has ten years of experience.
She uses AI **occasionally after review**, earns high manager pay and has eight months saved with plenty of similar offices nearby.
She and Jo have **two children** and a mortgage; Jo's garden design fees vary though planting is hands-on.
Fast AGI could hit **both desk incomes**, so she would test paid exhibit handling without assuming a gallery vacancy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce both her membership pay and Jo's garden design fees.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated staffing plan** and paid learning time before membership posts shrink.
A **posted exhibit-handling role** with enough pay for the mortgage and family costs.
